title: Mobile UX Constraints & Accessibility
summary: Thumbs, small screens, and screen readers impose constraints web accessibility rules don't fully cover. Learn touch ergonomics, TalkBack/VoiceOver basics, and permission timing.

slides.markdown:
A mouse cursor is a precise pixel; a thumb is a soft, imprecise pad covering a patch of screen, often reaching awkwardly across a device far taller than a hand is wide. That single physical difference is why mobile interaction design has its own rulebook, separate from desktop web usability.

This topic covers what's specific to a touch, small-screen device: sizing and placing targets for thumbs, gesture discoverability trade-offs, adapting across phones/tablets/foldables, and the on-device screen readers — TalkBack and VoiceOver — that make an app usable without sight. General web accessibility (ARIA, WCAG) lives in Web & Frontend; this is the mobile-specific layer on top of it.

slides.subTitle: Touch target size and reachability
slides.markdown:
A fingertip covers roughly a 40-48 point/dp patch of screen, far coarser than a mouse pointer, so both major platforms set a minimum touch target size (Apple recommends 44pt, Android 48dp) below which taps become unreliable — not because the visual element is too small to see, but because it's too small to reliably *hit*.

**Reachability** compounds this on today's larger phones: a one-handed grip can comfortably reach roughly the bottom half to two-thirds of the screen with a thumb, while the top corners require a grip shift or a second hand. That's why primary actions (a send button, a tab bar) cluster toward the bottom on modern phone UIs, while destructive or rare actions can live in the harder-to-reach top corners — reachability difficulty is a legitimate design tool for making a mistake harder to make accidentally.

A visually large button with a tiny actual tap area (padding excluded from the hit region) fails this even though it looks compliant — the hit area, not the visible icon, is what has to meet the minimum size.

slides.subTitle: Discoverability trade-offs
slides.markdown:
| | Button | Gesture |
|---|---|---|
| **Discoverability** | High — visible, self-explanatory | Low — invisible until learned or hinted |
| **Screen space** | Costs visible real estate | Free — no persistent UI element needed |
| **Accessibility** | Naturally exposed to screen readers | Requires deliberate extra work to expose (a labelled action alternative) |
| **Learning curve** | None | Real — first-time users often miss it entirely |

Gestures win on screen real estate and feel fluid once learned, which is why swipe-to-delete, pull-to-refresh, and edge-swipe navigation are everywhere on mobile. The trade-off is a genuine discoverability cost: a gesture with no visible affordance is invisible to a first-time user, and invisible entirely to someone using a screen reader unless you explicitly expose an equivalent action. The safest pattern for anything important is a gesture **plus** a discoverable button or menu item doing the same thing — never a gesture as the only path to a core action.

slides.sectionTitle: Adapting layout across phones, tablets, and foldables
slides.markdown:
A layout built and tested only on one phone size quietly assumes a screen width and aspect ratio that stops being true the moment the app runs on a tablet, a foldable's inner display, or even just a phone in landscape. The fix isn't a handful of fixed breakpoints copied from web design — it's designing layout in terms of **available space**, not device category: a list-detail pattern that shows just the list on a narrow width and both panes side by side once there's room, regardless of whether that room came from a tablet, a foldable unfolding, or a phone rotating.

Foldables add a wrinkle unique to mobile: the available width can change **while the app is running**, as the user unfolds the device mid-session, not just at launch. A layout that only recalculates on cold start will render wrong until the next relaunch — layout needs to react to a live size-class change, not just read it once.

The practical takeaway: test on the narrowest supported phone and the widest supported tablet/unfolded state, not just whatever device happens to be on the desk, since bugs at either extreme rarely show up in the middle.

slides.sectionTitle: Safe areas and responsive breakpoints on a device screen
slides.markdown:
Modern phone screens aren't a clean rectangle from the app's point of view — a notch or camera cutout, rounded corners, a home indicator bar, and (on foldables) a hinge seam all carve out **safe areas** that content must avoid to stay legible and tappable. Placing an interactive element flush against a raw screen edge risks it landing under a rounded corner or behind a system gesture area, where the OS intercepts the touch for its own edge gesture rather than passing it to the app.

Both platforms expose the safe-area insets programmatically specifically so layouts don't hardcode padding values that happen to work on today's device but break on next year's notch shape or corner radius. Combined with the space-based adaptation from the previous slide, the resilient approach is: respect safe-area insets as a floor, then let content reflow based on however much safe space is actually available, rather than a fixed pixel layout tuned to one specific device.

slides.subTitle: TalkBack and VoiceOver basics
slides.markdown:
TalkBack (Android) and VoiceOver (iOS) turn touch into an exploratory, audio-first interaction: a user swipes between elements one at a time, hearing each one's spoken label and role, and double-taps (rather than single-taps) to activate whatever's currently focused. This is a fundamentally different interaction model from sighted tapping, not just "tapping with narration added."

What makes an element usable this way: every interactive control needs an accessible **label** (what is this) and, where relevant, a **role/trait** (button, toggle, currently selected) and a **state** (checked, disabled) — all exposed through the platform's accessibility APIs, not just implied visually by an icon's shape or color. A custom-drawn control (a canvas-based slider, an icon-only button with no text) is invisible to a screen reader by default unless you explicitly attach that metadata; only standard platform widgets get it for free.

The test that catches most real gaps: turn the screen reader on and try to complete your app's core flow using only swipe-and-double-tap, no sighted shortcuts — issues that are invisible in a sighted code review surface immediately this way.

slides.sectionTitle: Asking for permissions at the moment they're needed
slides.markdown:
The same soft-ask principle from push notification permissions applies to every sensitive platform permission — location, camera, contacts, microphone: ask **in context**, right when the feature that needs it is about to be used, not in a batch during onboarding before the user has any reason to say yes.

A launch-time wall of permission requests ("this app would like to access: location, camera, contacts, microphone") with no context reads as suspicious even to users who'd happily grant each one individually when they understand why — and a denial here, like notification permission, is often effectively permanent without the user manually visiting settings. Asking for camera access the moment the user taps "scan a barcode," by contrast, has an obvious, immediate reason attached, and converts at a meaningfully higher rate.

The same pattern of explaining value first through your own UI, then triggering the real OS prompt only after the user opts in, applies across every sensitive permission on the platform, not just notifications — it's a general mobile UX principle, not a notification-specific trick.

slides.sectionTitle: A tap target visually bigger than its actual hit area
slides.markdown:
A button is styled with generous visual padding, looks comfortably large on screen, and still gets missed constantly by real users. The cause is almost always that the **visual bounds and the hit-testing bounds don't match** — the actual tappable region is only the inner icon or label, with the surrounding padding purely decorative and not part of the touch target at all.

This passes casual visual review because it genuinely looks fine, and it's exactly the kind of bug a developer testing with a precise mouse cursor or a careful, deliberate tap never reproduces — it shows up on a real thumb, in motion, on a moving bus, tapping slightly off-center from where a precise pointer would land dead center.

The fix is making sure the hit-testing region explicitly matches (or exceeds, via padding that's part of the tappable area, not just visual spacing) the platform's minimum touch target size, and testing with an actual finger on a real device rather than a mouse in a simulator, which trivially hits pixel-perfect targets a thumb never would.

slides.sectionTitle: An accessibility label that reads a decorative icon instead of its action
slides.markdown:
A trash-can icon button gets an accessibility label of `"trash icon"` or `"delete_24dp"` — technically a label exists, so a shallow audit checkbox passes, but a screen reader user hears a description of the *picture*, not what tapping it actually does.

This happens because the label often gets auto-derived from an image asset's filename or added as an afterthought to satisfy a linter, rather than authored to answer the question a screen reader user actually needs answered: "what happens if I activate this control right now?" The correct label here is something like `"Delete item"` — describing the **action**, not the icon, and ideally including enough context to disambiguate when several similar controls exist on the same screen ("Delete draft" vs. just "Delete" on a screen with three deletable things).

The same failure mode extends to decorative images that carry no information (a background flourish, a redundant icon next to text that already says the same thing) — those should be explicitly marked as decorative and skipped by the screen reader entirely, rather than read aloud and adding noise to every pass through the screen.
